view: A reported group of readers read mundhir with tanwin so that it governs its object; genitive attachment is also possible for lightness, though the governed construction is original.
note: The reading concerns a word in the neighboring passage, included here because its source note accompanies this verse.

view: Aisha reports that repeated questions about the Hour continued until verses 79:43–44 were revealed, after which the Prophet stopped asking about it; al-Hakim authenticated the report.
Tariq ibn Shihab reports that the Prophet often mentioned the Hour until verses 79:43–44 were revealed and then refrained from mentioning it.
A report promises that whoever recites Surat al-Nazi'at will be held in the grave and at Resurrection only as long as an obligatory prayer before entering Paradise.
note: Baydawi mentions only the resurrection interval and gives no grading.

view: Alusi rejects treating 'what place are you in regarding its reminder?' as a substitute for the question about the Hour or as the questioners' quoted words; the direct answer is that its endpoint belongs to God.
note: This concerns the connection of verses 42–44 to the closing comparison.

view: The Prophet's duty is to warn, while only God knows the Hour's endpoint; demands for its timing should not trouble him.
note: Ibn Jurayj glosses the endpoint as God's knowledge and the evening/morning as worldly time.

view: The closing verses answer disbelievers who taunted the Prophet for not knowing when the Hour would arrive.
The sura establishes resurrection and gathering and displays humanity's final fate after preceding suras' exposition; its oaths bring the matter to a decisive climax.
The name al-Nazi'at evokes angels extracting souls and the Moses–Pharaoh account; the names al-Sahirah and al-Tammah also suit the oaths and the sura's course.
The sura's close returns to resurrection from its opening and connects to the next sura through fear and remembrance.
note: The next-sura link mentions 80:1.

view: Depending on the contextual reading, the comparison is a circumstantial sentence or an independent sentence.
note: The grammatical choice follows whether it confirms the warning or answers the impatient challenge.

view: The people described are disbelievers, identified more specifically by some as the unbelievers of Quraysh or Mecca.
note: Some notes speak of people generally; these notes explicitly identify the deniers.

view: The scene conveys the Resurrection's great and many terrors; fear makes the stay in the grave or world seem short.
note: Some notes expressly give terror as the cause of the shortened impression.

view: The comparison brings the Hour close and answers those who impatiently ask when it will come: after the warning, their wait will seem brief, so its arrival should not be dismissed as distant.
note: Alusi presents swift arrival and rebuke of the mockers as contextual readings.

view: The cautious can escape the Hour's terrors, while the heedless face everlasting calamity.
The passage is used to reject the claim that afterlife comfort and pain are spiritual only, without sensation.
note: Qurtubi rejects the spiritual-only claim.

view: The evening or morning can signify truth's light setting in bodies or rising from the west; witnessing resurrection through unity makes worldly existence appear merely imagined.
Aisha reports that the Prophet told Bedouins asking about the Hour that, if the youngest visitor lived a century, their own Hour would have come.
Anas transmits a prayer asking for mercy, forgiveness, safety, good deeds, Paradise, and deliverance from Hell; it includes two verses about worldly time's brevity.
On seeing the Hour or Hereafter, people will perceive their worldly life as only an evening, a morning, or another very short part of a day, although their actual worldly stay was longer.
note: Other notes prefer the grave period; the alternatives remain separate below.

view: The brief sojourn is the time spent in the graves before resurrection; seeing the Resurrection's terror makes that interval seem only an afternoon or morning.
note: The sources differ on whether the short interval is worldly life or the grave stay; Study Quran attributes this view to most commentators.

view: The stay can encompass both life in the world and the ensuing time in the graves, together appearing no longer than part of a day when the Hour comes.
note: Tabataba'i describes worldly life until resurrection; Biqa'i expressly names the world and graves.

view: The grave period is preferable as the intended sojourn because people's entire worldly life is counted for judgment; the worldly-life reading is rejected on this ground.
note: This preference opposes the worldly-life interpretation; the author cites 23:114 in discussing it.

view: An alternative takes the sojourn as the interval from asking when the Hour will come until resurrection, but Tabataba'i rejects it: the interval is witnessed only at resurrection, and death rather than the question precedes it.
note: The proposed starting point of the interval is disputed.

view: Ibn Abbas, through al-Dahhak, says people will think they remained in the world for only one day.
note: This estimate is a full day, distinct from the part-day estimates.

view: The short apparent stay warns people that worldly pleasures will soon end and they will leave them as though they had remained only an evening or morning.
Against the endless afterlife, worldly time is negligible; one comparison likens this world's share to a finger dipped in the sea and withdrawn.
note: Biqa'i attributes the finger-and-sea comparison to the Prophet.

view: Disbelievers give differing estimates of how long they stayed, yet their past appears only a brief hour beside the endless future they face.
Earthly time is an illusory concept that loses its meaning in the ultimate reality of the Hereafter.
note: The note compares several Quranic passages about perceived time.

view: Psychologically, finished past time seems short, whereas the open, uncertain future feels more important and can provoke anxiety.
The short stay is compared with Quranic scenes where worldly life seems an hour or part of a day, particularly 10:45 and 46:35.
note: The cited parallels vary by source; the grave-stay view cites several further time-estimate verses.

view: The phrase recalls the judgment dialogue in al-Mu'minun: people are asked how many years they remained, answer a day or part of one, and defer to those who count.
note: Tabataba'i cites 23:114 while disputing the worldly-life interpretation.

view: Evening denotes the period from noon or afternoon until sunset, while forenoon or morning denotes the period from sunrise until noon; Muqatil describes the morning as lasting until the sun rises higher.
note: The precise morning endpoint differs slightly across the notes.

view: Arabic can pair an evening with the following morning, or a morning with its preceding evening; on this account 'its forenoon' can be the morning after the named evening.
note: These notes differ from those that locate the morning earlier on the same day; Wahidi's wording also associates it with the evening's day.

view: Evening has no literal forenoon; the Arabic expression pairs the end and beginning of a day to indicate one of its two ends, rather than a forenoon belonging literally to an evening.
note: The notes use beginning/end and morning/evening terminology for the idiom.

view: A verse by a poet of Banu Uqayl uses 'the evening of the new moon' for the evening of its setting or hidden phase; the citation supports the Arabic time-pairing idiom.
note: The reports vary in how they describe the moon's hidden phase.

view: The compact phrase expresses 'only an hour of a day, its evening or forenoon'; attaching 'its' makes the measure a part of one day, excluding a span from one day's evening to another day's forenoon.
note: The wording's brevity and the possessive carry the point.

view: Al-Tibi allows evening or forenoon to represent a whole day metaphorically, with the pronoun reinforcing that sense as in saying one saw something 'with one's own eyes.'
note: Other notes take the phrase as less than a whole day.

view: The estimated stay amounts to only part of one day, whether expressed as its evening or its morning.
note: This differs from the report estimating a full day.

view: The two short spans can signify bodily and spiritual worlds, concealed respectively by sensation and intellect; passing them is described as two steps before arrival.
Other Quranic uses of duha include the time opposite evening, sunlight brought forth, and a set time for events; these usages weigh against making it mean a whole day.
note: This challenges the whole-day reading.

view: On a report from Ibn Abbas through Ata, the final ha and alif are grammatical additions rather than a meaningful possessive; the sense is simply 'an evening or a morning.'
note: This differs from explanations that make the suffix refer to the evening.

view: The suffix refers to 'evening,' attaching the forenoon to that evening by their association within one day; Arabic can name the earlier morning through its later evening.
note: The notes ground the annexation in the periods' relation as two ends of one day.

view: Grammarians permit the possessive link on even a slight relation between times; one figurative application calls an ordeal its evening and relief its morning.
note: This extends the time-pairing beyond literal parts of a day.

view: Alusi prefers the simpler account of the added pronoun, while allowing that it could also reinforce al-Tibi's whole-day reading.
note: The disagreement turns on whether the possessive merely links the two periods or reinforces a metaphor for a whole day.

view: The attachment of forenoon to evening also serves the verse's cadence.
Some interpret the morning as representing worldly life as people see the Hereafter.
note: This is a symbolic reading of the morning rather than a clock-time definition.
